Unresolved source(s): Unnamed salt-stressed baker's yeast paper, referenced at 9:27 and 12:28 (not named in video or description) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Salt-stressed yeast accumulates glycerol (reported 2.8-fold over control) and in sweet dough gives faster fermentation, larger specific volume, softer crumb and lower firmness after storage; glycerol is proposed to lubricate gas cells and slow collapse.
conditions: sweet bread dough made with salt-stressed baker's yeast
notes: Figures are as read from the quoted paper; not verified against the original. Unresolved source(s): Same unnamed salt-stressed yeast paper (quoted 9:27-10:39); not named in video [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: In a steamed-bread study, matcha slowed early volume rise (up to 120 min), then doughs with matcha rose faster from about 150 min; higher matcha lowered total volume and prolonged fermentation. Sensory scores were highest at 4.5-6% matcha, and the authors suggested limiting matcha to about 6%.
conditions: steamed bread, not baked bread; percent base assumed to be flour weight
notes: Study is on steamed bread; she extrapolates to baked sweet bread. Percent base not stated in the video. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper on matcha in steamed bread (not named in video or description) [literature claim without an identifiable paper] Paper also found no significant sensory difference across 1.5–6% matcha (8:16).

claim: Tangzhong at 2:1 water to flour (70 g boiling water to 35 g bread flour, which is 20% of total flour) is made, cooled, then rested overnight in the fridge for fuller benefit.
notes: Her recipe ratio, not a measured optimum. Overnight rest is her preference (she says the tangzhong can be used immediately).

claim: About 25% of the water in the dough is replaced by milk, citing a scientific paper: 27 g milk in the dough plus 6 g in the yeast mix.
conditions: sweet milk bread dough with tangzhong
notes: Description states milk water replacement 23.4%; the 25% figure is the video's stated basis. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed scientific paper on water replacement with milk (not named in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: With a tangzhong dough, a cold, stiff tangzhong slows mixing. Butter is added only after about 6 min of kneading; kneading then continues about 5-6 min to near full development. After 15 min rest, slap-and-folds for about 5 min give a dough that passes the windowpane.
notes: Hand method. She states research shows tangzhong increases stand-mixer mixing time; the research is not named.

claim: Bake sweet tangzhong loaf at 175 C: 8 min on bottom heat only, then 15 min on top and bottom heat; proof until the dough sits a little above the pan rim.
conditions: 23x5.8x9.7 cm loaf pan, lined; oven type not stated
notes: Oven-specific settings; she checks core temperature but gives no target core temperature.

claim: Garlic (1% garlic powder) does not kill yeast in the cited study but weakens dough structure: a garlic compound (an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl) reacts with gluten, reducing elasticity and raising viscosity, which lowers volume and makes bread denser and harder with more garlic.
conditions: wheat bread dough with garlic powder
notes: Contradicts the common assumption that garlic harms bread by killing yeast. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed study on 1% garlic powder, yeast activity and dough structure (not named in video or description) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: In one Philippine study, adding freshly crushed garlic to bread extended shelf life by inhibiting mould growth.
notes: Single study, not named; the active component is attributed to allicin. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed Philippine study on garlic and bread shelf life (not named in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Adding garlic powder reduced acrylamide: 5 g garlic powder in 500 g wheat flour (1% of flour) gave a 45% reduction against a control, and more garlic gave more reduction; allicin and flavonoids are named as the active components.
conditions: bread dough, control without garlic powder
notes: Single study, not named; reduction measured against a single control recipe. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed study on garlic powder and acrylamide in bread (not named in video or description) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Sensory panels in two studies showed liking of garlic bread falls as garlic powder rises above about 1% of flour, with dislike of strong garlic taste; she caps garlic powder at 1% baker's percentage. One Korean panel of 20 students preferred 1% garlic powder slightly more than control.
conditions: bread with garlic powder; trained and untrained panels
notes: The studies are not named; the 1% cap is her synthesis. Cultural effects on panel results are acknowledged in the video. Unresolved source(s): Two unnamed sensory studies (4:42-5:19): a 9-person trained university panel, and a 20-student Korean panel [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Allicin forms only when garlic is cut or crushed (alliinase and alliin mix). Heat denatures alliinase, so cooked or dried garlic makes less allicin; garlic powder may yield less allicin than fresh garlic, and some sources quote up to about 50% alliin loss in powder.
notes: Enzyme and heat mechanism is standard garlic chemistry. The 50% figure is unsourced in the video; treat as low confidence on the number. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed sources quoted at 5:55 for the 50% alliin reduction in garlic powder [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Allicin is soluble in fat but not well dispersed in water, so fat such as butter spreads garlic flavour through the dough.
conditions: garlic in enriched dough with butter
notes: Her chemistry explanation for the design choice; no measurement shown.

claim: Garlic and tangzhong weaken the gluten structure but can make the dough stiffer and easier to shape and divide.
conditions: garlic and tangzhong dough, sausage roll recipe
notes: Her handling observation for this dough.

claim: Tangzhong made from 1:2 flour to boiling water (45 g bread flour to 90 g water, about 15% of total flour) is rested overnight; the rest lets flour amylases break the gelatinized starch into simpler sugars, which sweetens the bread.
conditions: bread flour tangzhong, rested a day before the dough
notes: Amylase sweetening is her explanation; not measured in the video.

claim: Tangzhong in this enriched dough is credited with a dough that keeps softer for longer, freezes better, tastes slightly sweeter, retains more water, and has a chewier, mochi-like texture.
conditions: enriched sweet dough with tangzhong and tapioca starch
notes: Summary of benefits she has covered in earlier videos; not individually tested here.

claim: Replacing part of the tapioca starch with wheat flour (original mochi-donut blend about 60% tapioca and 40% all-purpose flour, reduced in this recipe) adds gluten, makes the dough less sticky and gives fluffier rolls.
conditions: mochi-donut base adapted to cinnamon rolls
notes: Switching to bread flour is also part of this change; the effect is her stated reasoning.

claim: A lower-hydration rolled dough is easier to shape; pouring 60 g of milk over the rolls in the pan before proofing raises hydration in the pan and keeps the rolls soft.
conditions: cinnamon rolls baked in a lined pan
notes: Adapted from a viral hack that used heavy cream; not measured.

claim: Add instant yeast onto the dry ingredients rather than the liquids, so it is not in direct contact with the liquids during rehydration.
notes: Method rule; she references her earlier yeast video.

claim: Soft butter is added after about 3-4 min of mixing; the dough is then mixed about 5-6 more min to full gluten development, and passes the windowpane when it cleans the bowl and sides.
conditions: stand mixer on medium speed, enriched dough with about 25 g butter
notes: Fat timing: butter added after the initial gluten development, as she says it coats the flour proteins.

claim: Kansui (alkaline salt) at about 1% of flour weight adds springiness, yellow colour and alkalinity to noodle dough. Too much adds bitterness, odour and reduces springiness.
notes: Her practice, based on her own comparisons; no measurement shown.

claim: Thin noodles need a higher-protein flour so the dough is elastic enough to stretch; thicker noodles like udon use lower protein. Stronger dough gives firmer, chewier noodles, which suits thin noodles but can be too tough for thick ones.
notes: General principle; no protein percentages given.

claim: Noodle dough at about 40% hydration (water to flour) is high for noodles and is easier to knead and roll; wetter doughs give softer noodles, drier doughs give more bite.
conditions: thin Chinese noodles with high-protein bread flour
notes: Her recipe hydration; the trade-off statement is her general observation.

claim: Dissolve salt and kansui fully in the water, add the solution to the flour in small portions with mixing between, then rest sealed for 1 h, knead, rest 2 h, and knead until the dough does not tear. Longer rests make the dough easier to handle and better tasting.
notes: Replaces the traditional body-weight kneading of noodle dough; the flavour benefit of longer rests is her claim.

claim: Noodles are boiled in small batches for about 1-1.5 min with stirring; undercooked noodles taste soggy. Tossing them in oil right after cooking prevents sticking.
conditions: thin fresh noodles, boiling water with a little oil
notes: Cooking time is for her noodle thickness.

claim: Sourdough leavening must be mature and rise on a predictable schedule; a mature starter is needed for reliable gas production in the dough.
notes: General practice statement.

claim: Flour used in a tangzhong is largely denatured and contributes little dough strength; it can disturb the gluten network and reduce gas retention. Tangzhong doughs look drier and stronger than they are, so the windowpane test must be passed after mixing.
notes: Her observation. She calls the drier look an illusion.

claim: Acidic dough activates flour proteases, which can break gluten chains; if sourdough is left too long the dough can turn into a slurry.
notes: Consistent with claim s08-007 on proteolysis.

claim: More steam during baking gives a lighter, glossier crust (starch gelatinizes, dextrinizes and caramelizes at the surface) and also a more brittle crust, with higher puncture failure force.
notes: Paper not identified in the transcript or description. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper(s) on steaming during baking, with crust colour, gloss and puncture tests (not named in video; 7:11-8:27) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Low steam lets the crust set early, so internal pressure splits it and forms an ear or tears; high steam keeps the surface moist and expandable, giving a smooth surface with no ear. Too much steam gives a higher loaf volume but no ear.
conditions: loaves baked in an oven with varying steam; the study loaves were unscored
notes: The mechanism linking this paper to ears is her inference; she says the paper does not mention ears. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper on steaming and specific volume of bread (quoted 9:08-11:44; not named) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: A reference upper limit of about 400 mL steam injected in one study equates to about 1.33 L of steam per cubic metre of oven, or roughly 1.3 mL per litre of oven volume, before accounting for evaporation through the oven walls and door.
conditions: domestic oven; evaporation not accounted for
notes: Generalised from her own worked example, which used a personal oven volume; the per-litre rate is the transferable figure. The study's oven volume is implied, not stated. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed earlier paper on steam and bread crust (13:38; not named) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Covering the loaf (loaf pan or Dutch oven) traps the water the bread releases; the dough loses about 10-20% of its initial mass as water during baking, which can supply steam in a small covered space.
conditions: covered baking in a small volume
notes: The 10-20% range is narrated without a source.

claim: Score with the blade at about 45 degrees and a deep first cut, then go back in at a more horizontal angle to make a flap that separates and opens as an ear. Chilled dough scores more easily but has trade-offs during baking.
notes: Technique statement; the angle is hers.

claim: Under-proofing and over-proofing both cause defects; over-proofed dough collapses in the oven, under-proofed dough gives gaping holes and a gummy crumb. She prefers a slight under-proof over an over-proof.
notes: Her preference, not a measured rule.

claim: Spent coffee grounds at 10% of flour weight (about 11% baker's percentage) gave the best aroma and hardness in one shortbread study; in a cookie study 10-20% of flour gave acceptable sensory scores, while 25% increased hardness and reduced acceptability. Cookies with at least 10% grounds were classed as high fibre.
conditions: dried and finely sieved spent coffee grounds replacing wheat flour
notes: Studies not named in the transcript; the cookie-study match is inferred. The difference between studies may be due to fat content, which she notes. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed shortbread study with spent coffee grounds (3:32)

claim: Biscuits made with spent coffee grounds increased satiety and reduced ad libitum energy intake in healthy overweight volunteers in a pilot study; biscuits were well tolerated.
conditions: pilot study with healthy overweight volunteers; biscuit form
notes: Pilot-scale evidence; she states more research is needed. The study title is in the description; the link is inferred.

claim: Use a low-protein cake flour for cookies, so that little gluten forms during mixing.
notes: Standard cookie practice as she states it.

claim: Spent coffee grounds should be dried thoroughly, then finely ground and sieved; coarse grounds make cookies gritty.
conditions: spent coffee grounds in cookie dough
notes: Both referenced studies dried and sieved the grounds.

claim: Chilling cookie dough (a log for about 45 min, then shaped pieces for about 1 h) makes it firm enough to shape and keeps it from spreading in the oven; a brief re-chill helps if it gets sticky.
conditions: butter-based cookie dough with icing sugar
notes: Her handling practice; the no-spread effect is her statement.

claim: A poolish of equal weights bread flour and fruit yeast water, matured 12-18 h at room temperature until domed and dimpled (15 h shown), is the starter for this no-knead herb loaf.
notes: Timing depends on room temperature.

claim: No-knead high-hydration dough is developed with four sets of stretch-and-folds (four folds per set, one per side) with 45 min rests between sets, then rested 45 min. Folding is gentler and more convenient than kneading for high-hydration dough.
notes: Wet hands are used to prevent sticking; dough strength is judged by how it holds shape and jiggles.

claim: Retarding the shaped dough in the fridge for 4-8 h (6 h shown) improves flavour through slower fermentation and enzyme activity, and makes the dough easier to score because there is less drag.
conditions: shaped boule in a covered container; fridge temperature not stated
notes: Flavour and scoring effects are her observations.

claim: Bake a covered loaf in a lidded casserole at 250 C for 35 min, then uncovered for 20 min. The lid keeps the crust soft early so the loaf can expand; a small bowl of water in the oven gives similar steam.
conditions: glass lidded casserole, preheated oven; oven type not stated
notes: Oven settings are hers and need adjusting per oven.

claim: Cool the loaf to room temperature before cutting; cutting hot bread ruins the crumb and makes it gummy.
notes: Standard practice as she states it.

claim: For mini baguettes, a poolish of fruit yeast water and bread flour (1:1) matured about 11 h; 200 g of this poolish is used in a dough with 150 g more flour, giving about 40% of total flour in the poolish.
notes: Maturation time depends on temperature.

claim: Bulk fermentation uses four sets of stretch-and-folds (four per set) 45 min apart; total bulk runs about 3-5 h depending on room temperature, fruit yeast water activity and target dough temperature. Stop folding when the dough gets hard to stretch.
notes: Duration is conditional on temperature, which the video does not fix.

claim: Pre-shape the dough into even pieces without degassing, then bench rest 30-45 min before final shaping so the dough relaxes enough to shape.
notes: Shaping practice; no dough temperature given.

claim: Proof baguettes on a cloth dusted with corn starch for 1-1.5 h until doubled; bake at a very high oven temperature (260 C in her oven) with water sprayed on the dough for steam, scored just before baking, for 30 min.
conditions: mini baguettes; oven settings are hers
notes: Temperatures are set on her oven; she says to adjust to your oven.

claim: Butter is added after the dough has begun to develop gluten, because fat coats the flour proteins and blocks network formation. Add softened butter on low for 1-2 min, then on medium for 8-10 min until smooth and windowpane-ready.
conditions: stand mixer, dough hook, enriched milk loaf
notes: Fat timing: the dough looks like it has come apart at first, which is normal.

claim: Milk powder adds milk solids and flavour without adding much liquid; adding the liquid milk first helps the poolish dissolve.
notes: Method reasoning.

claim: Milk loaf rolls are bulk fermented about 3 h to double, bench rested 25 min, shaped into rolls in a buttered pan, and proofed 2-3 h until risen, then baked with 10 min on bottom heat and 25-35 min on top and bottom heat.
conditions: buttered loaf pan; proof height not quantified
notes: Preheat stated as 185 C but bake stated at 190 C in the transcript; baked covered or open at preference.

claim: A 75% hydration no-knead loaf uses 200 g bread flour with 150 g fruit yeast water, mixed only until homogeneous; the dough stays shaggy and tears when stretched, which is intended.
conditions: no-knead loaf with fruit yeast water
notes: Hydration as stated in title and ingredients.

claim: No-knead dough gets three to four rounds of stretch-and-folds (one per side) with 45 min rests, a 45 min rest before pre-shaping, a 20 min bench rest, and about 2 h of proof until doubled.
notes: Rounds depend on dough strength, room temperature and humidity, as she says.

claim: Dough is ready to bake when a floured fingertip poke leaves an indent that springs back slowly, leaving a mark.
notes: Poke test as described.

claim: Calvel's autolyse (a rest after mixing flour and water, before the rest of the mix) improved starch-gluten-water links, cut total mixing time by about 15% (less oxidation), and gave a more supple crumb with better cell structure.
conditions: Traditional French white-bread method as described by Calvel; creator's account of his experiments
notes: Creator's paraphrase of Calvel's experiments; the original study was not checked.

claim: Calvel attributed the decline of French bread quality (from about 1957 to 1969) mainly to intensive mechanical mixing and the hyper-oxidation of dough it caused.
conditions: Historical French artisan context, mid-20th century
notes: Historical attribution as presented by the creator; not independently verified.

claim: Lipid oxidation starts in the first minutes of mixing: yeast respiration and flour lipoxygenase compete for dissolved oxygen, producing aldehydes and ketones that taste stale or rancid. It happens in lean doughs without added fat.
conditions: Lean wheat dough, first minutes of mixing
notes: Source of this passage is inferred from the description reference list.

claim: In a review comparing industrial, artisan and homemade soft breads, industrial bread had fewer fruity esters (e.g. ethyl octanoate), more aldehydes and furans (lipid oxidation), and more Maillard products (e.g. 2,5-dimethylpyrazine). Artisan bread had more esters, consistent with stronger fermentation; homemade bread had fewer Maillard products.
conditions: Soft-bread recipes compared across industrial, artisanal and homemade categories
notes: Category-level differences from a review, not a controlled home-baking test. Industrial 'soft bread' means commercial sandwich-type loaves.

claim: A traditional French process with softer, wetter dough, longer fermentation and more yeast gave baguettes scoring higher in porosity, elasticity, crust crispness, crackle, volume and fresh flavour than a stiffer industrial process. Wetter doughs also stay softer longer.
conditions: Baguettes; traditional soft dough vs industrial stiff dough
notes: Confounded: the traditional process also used more yeast and longer fermentation (creator says so). Hydration effect not isolated in the video.

claim: Adding more baker's yeast shortens bulk fermentation but gives a pronounced yeasty taste, less flavour, and faster staling.

Calvel considered ascorbic acid (vitamin C) a harmless auxiliary that reinforces dough tenacity and tolerance and reduces over-oxidation. He rejected fava and soy flour because their lipoxygenase, combined with intensive mixing, destroys flavour and bleaches the crumb.
notes: Conflicts with the 1993 French Bread Decree as described in s09-008, which bans ascorbic acid.

claim: The 1993 French Bread Decree defines bread in the French tradition as made only from bread flour, water, salt and yeast or sourdough. It bans additives such as ascorbic acid, lecithin and fava flour, and restricts the term boulangerie to on-site production by qualified bakers.
notes: Legal rule as stated by the creator; verify against the decree text before citing in the app.

claim: Health benefits attributed to sourdough may come from other ingredients such as whole grain, fibre or ancient grains rather than the sourdough itself. Sourdough-labelled industrial loaves with a little starter and much sugar are unlikely to be healthier.
notes: Creator's summary of a review; not checked.

claim: Resting tangzhong refrigerated for about 8 h (overnight in her practice) lets wheat amylases break starch into maltose and other reducing sugars, adding sweetness and wheat flavour. She notes many references suggest 24 h or longer.
conditions: Tangzhong made with bread flour and boiling water
notes: Mechanism given by the creator without a named source for the sweetness effect. Her overnight rest is her practice, not a measured optimum.

claim: Soaking tangzhong in the dough water for about 5 minutes breaks up gelatinized clumps, so no-knead high-hydration dough takes it in evenly; otherwise chunks of starch can remain and interfere with gluten.
notes: Repeated at 22:36 with the same practice.

claim: Flour heated in a tangzhong has its proteins denatured, so that flour contributes essentially no gluten strength to the dough.
notes: Stated without a cited source.

claim: An organic acid added to flour raised water absorption about 1% but roughly halved dough development time; the paper concluded that acid substantially decreased mixing time and weakened the dough. This is relevant to sourdough, which is acidic.
notes: Figures read aloud from the paper; the paper itself was not identified. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper on organic acids and salt in wheat-flour dough (not named in video or description) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: In flour treated with organic acid, 1.5% salt (baker's %) raised mixing time by 8.3 min versus 0.8 min at 1.0% salt, and salt with acid greatly increased dough strength. Reducing salt by 0.5% is critical for mixing time when acids are present.
notes: Passage quotes water-absorption values that look inconsistent (1.5% salt lower absorption than 1.0%); not verified. The dose sensitivity is the usable point. Unresolved source(s): Same unnamed paper on organic acids and salt in flour (not identified) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Scaling the paper's 1.5% salt (for 11%-protein flour) to 13%-protein bread flour gives about 1.7%. She uses 1.75% salt on flour weight in her sourdough recipe.
notes: Her own proportional scaling; not measured.

claim: Wheat starch gelatinizes around 65 °C in excess water. A 1:1 flour-to-boiling-water mix (yudane or tangzhong) exceeds the water needed. Gelatinized starch then retrogrades and can release liquid (syneresis) when refrigerated around 4 °C.
notes: General food-science explanation without a cited source.

claim: Using starter directly in place of a levain would need about 100 g of starter for 400 g flour at 100% hydration, using a 1:4:4 starter:flour:water dilution that gives about three doubling generations. That is five times the 20 g used for the levain.
notes: Based on her earlier sourdough video's dilution logic; the arithmetic is hers.

claim: A levain of 20 g starter, 40 g flour and 40 g water that rises to at least double in 5 to 6 h gives leavening power comparable to about 100 g of starter. It also lets the baker keep a small starter and change its flavour.
notes: 'Equivalent to 100 g starter' is her dilution arithmetic (see s09-017).

claim: A new sourdough starter usually reaches maturity after about 5 to 7 days of regular feeding.
notes: No study named; treat as general guidance. Unresolved source(s): 'Research shows' (unnamed in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Bake the tangzhong sourdough in a Dutch oven with the lid on at 250 °C for 25 min, then at 210 °C until done. Tangzhong doughs need extra time so the moister crumb dries and sets.
conditions: Dutch oven; final time depends on oven
notes: Second-stage time not given; oven-dependent.

claim: Tangzhong complements sourdough: its sweetness balances sourdough acidity and improves flavour and texture. This contradicts the common view that tangzhong adds nothing to sourdough, because sourdough already slows staling.
notes: Contradicts common advice that tangzhong is pointless in sourdough; she attributes that view to focusing only on staling.

claim: Salt slows yeast growth, so a dough with enough salt can take roughly double the proofing time.
conditions: Lean dough, salt vs no salt
notes: No specific study named at this point; subjective demo with two doughs.

claim: Salt tightens gluten by letting gluten bond to itself rather than to water, giving a stronger network that retains more gas. Dough without salt was stickier and weaker in her hand-mixed comparison, and the stickiness effect of a 50% salt cut was described as significant in a study.
conditions: Hand-mixed lean dough, with and without salt
notes: Demo is subjective, per creator. Mechanism is her explanation. Unresolved source(s): 'It has been shown' study on 50% salt cut and stickiness (unnamed) Home side-by-side comparison shown in the video (single trial, not a controlled study).

claim: Salt-free bread had larger air cells than salted bread, and was significantly harder after about 120 h (5 days), with no significant hardness difference at 2 to 50 h. Salt-free bread tasted more sour, acidic and yeasty.
conditions: Bread with no salt vs salted bread, study conditions
notes: Study not identified; the description's references are the closest candidates but none confirmed. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed study on salt-free lean bread (not identified in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Salt has different effects on the two sourdough microbes: up to about 0.7% salt stimulates lactic acid bacteria, while higher levels suppress them much more strongly than yeast. Build a levain before adding a starter to a salted dough.
notes: Source identity inferred from description references.

claim: Water activity is what salt lowers; typical bread sits at about 88 to 95% equilibrium relative humidity, which makes it prone to microbial spoilage. Salt is about 11 times more effective than sugar at lowering water activity in equal amounts.
conditions: Bread, equal weights of salt and sugar
notes: 11x figure stated without a named source in the segment.

claim: Lowering salt in a lean bread from 1.2% to 0.6%, 0.3% and 0.0% shortened shelf life by about 2 days (from about 5-6 days to 3-4 days) under controlled conditions. The bread was exposed to the bakery air for only 10 min before bagging.
conditions: Controlled study conditions; bread exposed 10 min to bakery air before bagging
notes: Study identity inferred from description references. Home shelf life will differ.

claim: With sourdough, shelf life extended to 12 to 14 days compared with the control, and the salt level no longer significantly changed shelf life. The study used a specific antifungal, so results may vary with starter.
conditions: Salt-reduced bread with sourdough and an antifungal
notes: Creator says the antifungal limits direct transfer to home sourdough.

claim: Some studies show MSG improves the flavour of salt-reduced bread, especially with spices. A 2022 study found no significant difference in liking with or without MSG, and that study was partly funded by an MSG manufacturer.
conditions: Salt-reduced bread with and without MSG
notes: Funding conflict noted by the creator. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed 2022 study on MSG in salt-reduced bread (not named in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: In a Dutch in-home study, consumers given salt-reduced soy-sauce bread at first liked it less than regular bread for the first 5 days, but from day 6 there was no significant difference. Liking of the soy bread with sweet fillings rose most.
conditions: Weekday exclusive consumption, bread eaten with fillings
notes: Creator notes the study was in the Netherlands; liking may differ elsewhere.

claim: A one-quarter reduction in bread salt can be made without detection by consumers by cutting 5% steps over 6 weeks.
notes: No flavour or liking differences in the follow-up period, per creator.

claim: A 52% salt reduction in brown bread over 4 weeks of buffet breakfasts did not increase sodium from sandwich fillings. Consumption fell at a 67% reduction, but not when the bread was compensated with potassium chloride and yeast extract.
notes: Potassium chloride is sold as a salt substitute; the study's fillings were ham-heavy per creator.

claim: Longer proofing makes bread taste saltier: coarser, larger pores release sodium faster in the mouth. Pores that become too large make the crumb lumpy and slow sodium release.
conditions: Bread proofed for longer vs shorter or not at all
notes: Creator's summary.

claim: Reducing salt may make the crumb coarser, which could increase perceived saltiness. The creator explicitly labels this as speculation.
notes: Speculation combining claims s09-024 and s09-033, flagged as such by the creator.

claim: Layering doughs with different salt contents (inhomogeneous salt distribution) gave a 28% salt reduction with no loss of saltiness intensity. For bread at 1.8% salt on flour, that means below 1.3%. The effect was weaker on a trained panel and worked for about 31% of consumers in a 2019 study.
conditions: Sheets of doughs at different salt levels rolled and layered before baking
notes: The 2019 study is not named in the video; description ref 19 may be related but is unconfirmed.

claim: Tapioca starch clumps easily and absorbs water quickly. Mix it into the liquids as a sieved slurry before adding flour; sieving helps in humid climates where lumps form in storage.
conditions: Humid climate; tapioca starch added to bread dough

claim: Tapioca starch has no gluten and competes with proteins for water, so the dough needs extra water and becomes wetter and tackier. In lamination-built dinner rolls this is acceptable.
conditions: Tapioca starch at about 23% of total flour

claim: About 23% tapioca starch of total flour was the best level in her tests for soft rolls. Cassava flour, which carries more fibre, thickens more, so more starch is needed to match it.
conditions: Soft dinner rolls; her own tests
notes: Her internal tests; no data shown.

claim: In a study replacing 20% of wheat flour with high-quality cassava flour, a sensory panel accepted the blend. Cassava breads had higher bacterial and fungal loads, higher pH and moisture, and probably shorter shelf life than 100% wheat bread.
conditions: Whole cassava flour, not tapioca starch; home fermentation times differ
notes: Creator warns cassava flour is not tapioca starch, so relevance here is limited.

claim: Gluten can be built with two laminations separated by 20-minute rests instead of stretch-and-folds. She states this development needs about 15% of the energy of normal gluten building.
notes: The 15% energy figure is from the creator and was not verified against the source. Unresolved source(s): Noll B., 2010, On the track of dough development (description ref 1) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Lowering instant yeast from her usual 1% baker's to about 0.7% (2 g on 300 g flour) is enough when the dough rests between laminations, because yeast keeps multiplying through bulk fermentation.
notes: Timing varies with room temperature, per creator.

claim: Add instant yeast on top of the flour, after the liquids, sugar, salt and tangzhong. She says this helps instant yeast survive rehydration.
conditions: Instant yeast in an enriched dough

claim: Tangzhong must be mixed quickly while the water is hot enough, above about 65 °C, so the starch fully gelatinizes. Insufficient heat leaves starch holding less water, and the dough becomes sticky. Making tangzhong the night before and refrigerating it gives the best results.
notes: Her 1:2 ratio differs from the 1:5 ratio she discusses in other videos.

claim: A tangzhong made from 20% of flour makes a 100%-hydration dough handle like about 80% hydration. Tangzhong raises dough tenacity but does not strengthen gluten, so a windowpane test is still needed.
notes: Creator's rough calculation from a paper estimate; not measured in the video. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper's estimate (not identified)

claim: Tangzhong doughs need longer proofing, and at very high hydration the poke test can mislead. Underproofing, with tunnelling and a gummy crumb, is then a risk.
notes: Repeated at 21:58.

claim: Tangzhong mixes in more slowly because of its colloidal state. In no-knead dough, break chunks apart by hand in the water first to avoid uncombined pockets.
notes: Source not identified; practical advice. Unresolved source(s): 'Studies show' (unnamed in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: For a one-day or overnight ciabatta, a poolish at 100% hydration is preferred over a biga because it ferments faster. Ferment it with a tiny yeast dose and use it at its peak, when it has risen highest and begins to recede, for best flavour and gassing power.
notes: Yeast 0.6 g (1/8 tsp, 0.24% of flour); no extra yeast in the final dough.

claim: In tangzhong, enzyme action turns part of the damaged starch into maltose, giving mild natural sweetness and a wheat flavour. Together with the gelatinized starch, this helps bread stay fresh longer.
conditions: Tangzhong in lean or enriched dough

claim: A Japanese paper showed that gelatinized starch in pizza dough improves crust texture and moisture retention in home-oven pizza, giving a soft interior with a crisp exterior.
conditions: Home ovens versus very hot pizzeria ovens
notes: Paper not identified. Unresolved source(s): A Japanese paper on gelatinized starch in pizza dough (not named in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Spraying the shaped loaves with water just before the 250 °C bake of about 30 min helps the crust become crisp.
conditions: Parchment on a pan used as a peel; home oven
notes: Oven settings depend on the oven, per creator.

claim: For enriched white bread like shokupan, upper limits of about 6% sugar, 10% honey powder, 25% of milk replaced with water, and 5-6% total fat give the best volume, texture and taste. Going above these lowers quality.
conditions: Shokupan and enriched white bread; percentages assumed to be of flour
notes: Creator's summary of unnamed papers. Milk-to-water wording is unclear and the flour basis is assumed. Unresolved source(s): 'Scientific papers' per creator (not named in video; likely covered in her earlier shokupan videos) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Well-made enriched white bread like shokupan stays soft and fresh longer and tastes better the next day.
conditions: Shokupan within the sugar and fat limits
notes: Opinion of the creator.

claim: A 1:1 flour-to-boiling-water tangzhong still gelatinizes well because it is above the minimum excess water. Keep the mixture above 65 °C while mixing, then rest it overnight refrigerated.
conditions: Tangzhong of 50 g flour and 50 g boiling water
notes: Uses a 1:1 ratio because of the quantity of water allocated for this recipe.

claim: A 100%-hydration poolish fermented for about 2 h and then refrigerated overnight is used for flavour rather than gas. Extra instant yeast is therefore added to the final dough.
conditions: Poolish of 50 g flour, 50 g water, 1/8 tsp yeast; fermentation time depends on room temperature

claim: Whole eggs increase dough strength and bread volume, and their interaction with salt makes eggs more functional in these roles.
notes: Mechanism deferred by the creator to another video.

claim: With no long fermentation to develop gluten, this dough needs full gluten development from the mixer. Check with a windowpane test before bulk fermentation.
conditions: Stand mixer, dough hook; about 3-4 min then 4-5 min after butter

claim: Add soft butter after initial gluten development. The dough seems to fall apart at first, then comes together and becomes smooth after 4-5 min more mixing, with a clean bowl base.
conditions: Butter added after the first mix on medium-high speed

claim: Proof shaped buns until they are almost twice their original volume (about 70 min). Underproofing gives dense buns, and overproofing makes them swell and collapse.
conditions: Burger buns of about 80 g; proofing time depends on room temperature

claim: Brush the buns with an egg-and-milk wash and sprinkle sesame, then bake at 180 °C for 12 min top and bottom, then 150 °C for 8 min. The wash browns through Maillard reaction; she expects the internal temperature to stay below about 90 °C.
conditions: Top and bottom heat, middle rack
notes: Core temperature is her expectation, not a measured target.

claim: These buns stay soft and get slightly sweeter over time, so they can be made ahead.
Flour with ash at or below 0.50% suits white mantou. Lower ash means fewer bran specks and whiter steamed buns. She uses flour with ash below 0.47% and protein of 10.5-11.5%.
conditions: Northern-style mantou made from flour alone
notes: She refers to research papers without naming them.

claim: Desired dough temperature sets the water temperature: water = 3 x desired dough temperature - flour temperature - room temperature - friction temperature. In hot, humid conditions the water is iced.
conditions: Hot, humid climate; ice water 105-110 g
notes: Standard dough-temperature formula, as used by the creator.

claim: Yellowing comes from high dough pH, such as from baking powder or soda, which activates flour xanthophyll pigments. Hard water and clumps of leavener cause yellow spots. Unpigmented white mantou needs neither.
Under-proofing gives a dense crumb and a dull skin, while over-proofing gives an uneven crumb and shrinkage. Proof about 30 min at 29 °C until doubled.
conditions: Creator's ambient 29 °C; the 30 min applies only at that temperature
notes: Timing is temperature-dependent.

claim: Over-kneading, a very strong flour or hard water can make gluten too strong, and the steamed bun shrinks after steaming.
notes: Knead until smooth, shiny and non-sticky, without over-kneading.

claim: Degas the dough thoroughly. Air trapped during mixing rises to the surface in the steamer and creates blisters.

Steam pressure too high causes blisters, and too low gives low quality. Use a bamboo steamer, lower the heat to medium after the water boils, leave a gap in the lid, and wrap the lid in cloth to absorb condensation.
conditions: Bamboo steamer; metal steamers need more care

claim: Opening the steamer lid too quickly cools the buns suddenly, so they lose internal pressure, shrink and wrinkle. Wait about 5 min after steaming before opening.
conditions: After steaming, metal or bamboo steamer
notes: The 5 min wait is stated at 5:37.

claim: Gummy mantou comes from damp flour, over-long fermentation (including starting buns in a cold steamer that warms and over-ferments), too low steam, and too short steaming.

Stovetop tangzhong: 1 part flour to 5 parts water, heated on low with constant stirring to 60-65 °C, then removed from heat and cooled in a bowl covered with film touching the surface. It can be used at once or refrigerated; she observed no change after more than a week.
notes: Her description of another video links 'Tangzhong 1:5 is a bad idea' (cDBh6i-NoVE description); that video was not read here.

claim: Yudane (the Japanese original): pour boiling water over flour at 1:1 and mix immediately. Warm the bowl with boiling water first, pour in the water before the flour, and use at once or refrigerate.
Starch gelatinization needs at least about 60 °C in her guide (she recommends 60-65 °C for tangzhong). If the water cools below that, the starch does not gelatinize and yudane stays sticky.
notes: Other videos on her channel give 65 °C as the gelatinization temperature; both figures appear.

claim: Yudane aged 3 days in the fridge developed a small but noticeable gluten-related difference compared with fresh yudane, with little visible effect on the bread.
notes: Single comparison, no measurement shown. Home side-by-side comparison shown in the video (single trial, not a controlled study).

claim: Stovetop tangzhong and poured yudane gave very similar results in her trials, with barely any differences.
conditions: Her test bakes; no measurements shown
notes: Trial results not quantified.

claim: Tangzhong and yudane use the same Chinese and Japanese characters (湯種). Yudane is the older Japanese technique, and the term tangzhong spread in English through Yvonne Chen's book '65 Degrees Celsius Tangzhong Bread'.
notes: Historical claim as stated by the creator.

claim: Fruit-yeast-water poolish: equal weights of bread flour and fruit yeast water, fermented 10 to 18 h covered, to leaven the dough without instant yeast.
conditions: No instant yeast; fruit yeast water

claim: Enclose frozen butter in a small dough wrapper (about 10 g) and pinch the seams tightly, so the butter does not leak out of the bun in the oven.

Add soft room-temperature butter after the dough is cohesive. The dough separates first, then absorbs the butter after 2-3 min more; mix until smooth and it passes windowpane (about 9-10 min on her mixer).
A 20-min bench rest relaxes the gluten, not to rise, so small buns shape more easily.
Final proof for about 2 h, covered with plastic, until the buns are about 1.5 times their original size.
notes: Proof time depends on temperature.

claim: Bake at 190 °C for 25 to 30 min. If the buns shrink at the check, they are underbaked; turning the oven back on can save them, with some wrinkling of the skin.
With no chemical leavener, fruit-yeast-water poolish is the only leavening. Dough must be strong enough to pass windowpane; if not, large bubbles form and split during frying.
Youtiao dough can be cold-fermented in the fridge for 16 to 20 h, or kneaded in a mixer and then fermented for about 4 h. Both routes need the dough to pass windowpane.
Frying oil at 160-175 °C puffs youtiao well. Too cold gives greasy, under-puffed sticks; too hot browns the outside while the inside stays raw. Fry 3-4 min, turning.
Stretch the strips to 1.5 to 2 times their length before frying, without tearing. The pan diameter caps the length; she cuts 13-15 cm strips for a pan of about 24 cm.
A mix of bread flour and all-purpose flour (90 g and 30 g) gives youtiao that are crisp outside and chewy inside.
notes: Her taste judgement; no comparison shown.

claim: Stale youtiao can be re-crisped in an oven at 180 °C for 5 to 10 min.

Egg white is about 90% water and 10% protein with no fat. Yolk is about 50% water, with fats, proteins and lecithin, a natural emulsifier. Yolk fat tenderizes and increases volume, which is why yolk-only recipes are richer and fluffier.
notes: Composition figures stated without a source.

claim: Eggs are mostly water and their size varies, so weigh eggs to know how much water they add. Several eggs can make dough sticky.
Fat, including yolk fat, interferes with gluten development and lengthens mixing. Add fat later or in portions to speed up the process.
Egg white proteins seem to make dough stronger and the crumb denser.
notes: Stated tentatively ('seem to') by the creator.

claim: A watery or loose tangzhong usually reflects too low a temperature while it is made. Starch needs excess water near 65 °C to gelatinize; a 1:1 flour-to-water ratio is enough, so temperature is the variable to fix.
conditions: Cooler kitchens cool the water faster; creator's kitchen is warm (27-30 °C)

claim: Add the hot water first, then the flour, and mix to hydrate it within about a minute. Adding water in portions cools the mix. In cool rooms, preheat the bowl with hot water and discard it before starting.
Strong, high-protein bread flour is unsuitable for steamed buns: it overextends in proof and tightens during steaming, giving shrinkage, wrinkles or dimples.
notes: Paraphrase of a quoted paper. Contradicts common advice that bread flour is the default for all breads. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper on steamed bread flour quality (cited in video; title/authors not given) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Cake flour is not a good substitute for steamed bread: it gives weak elasticity and chewiness and an overly white colour.
All-purpose flour gives a slightly yellow mantou; to imitate low-protein bao flour, replace 10-20% of the all-purpose flour with cornstarch.
notes: Her own description says commercial low-price bao flours are made this way. Colour is partly from flour bran/ash, cited to Lin et al., 1990 (video at 10:07).

claim: Standard yeast rate for steamed bread is 1% baker's percent of compressed yeast; use about one third of that for instant yeast (about 0.33%) and halve it again for a two-step (sponge-and-dough) method.
notes: Rates are the creator's conversions. The 1/3 and 1/2 factors are her rules of thumb, not measured.

claim: About 6% sugar (flour basis) is enough to feed yeast for roughly 3 hours of fermentation in steamed bread; the sugar is for the yeast, not for sweetness.
notes: Cited study not named in the video; the 3-hour figure is her reading of it. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed research on sugar and softness of steamed bread (video states softness rises up to about 2% sugar) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Salt is rarely used in steamed bread; when used, it stays below 0.5% of flour weight.
notes: Contradicts her Western-bread habit of about 1.5% salt; she says that level would make the dough too strong for steamed bread. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper quoted in video on salt in steamed bread [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Target a dough pH of about 6.4-6.7 for mantou. Over-acid dough gives a grey, small, dense, sour bun; too much alkali gives yellow colour and an alkali smell.
notes: No source named for the pH range.

claim: In steaming, most volume gain (steamer spring) happens in the first 5 minutes; steam must reach full heat (about 12 minutes to reach maximum temperature); leave the buns covered for 5 minutes after steaming before opening the lid to avoid shrinkage.
conditions: steamer lid closed; steam flowing before dough goes in
notes: Steaming times depend on the steamer; she advises finding the right heat setting for your own steamer. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed book on steamed bread cited in video [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Blisters on steamed bread come from air bubbles trapped during mixing that were not removed by degassing; they appear at the surface in the first minutes of steaming.
Pita puffs only if the internal temperature reaches at least 100 C, so the water turns to steam and the bread is fully baked.
conditions: flatbread cooked in a hot pan
notes: The puff needs a strong gluten network, enough CO2 and steam, and rolling thin enough but not too thin.

claim: For a lean pita dough with tangzhong, limit the scalded flour to under 15% of total flour (not the 20% she uses for other lean doughs) to protect the gluten network.
notes: Contradicts her own usual 20% tangzhong guidance for lean doughs (stated in the same video). Safety margin, not a measured optimum.

claim: Pita needs about 71% hydration: enough water for steam to puff the bread, and tangzhong makes the wet dough easier to knead.
notes: Her figure. Recipe total water 250 g on 350 g flour = 71.4%.

claim: A poolish of equal flour and water with a trace of instant yeast can rest 2 h at room temperature and then go overnight in the fridge, for more flavour and better texture; 4 h at room temperature is the one-day alternative.
No extra sugar is added to this lean pita: the poolish's long rest breaks down proteins into flavour precursors, and the tangzhong starch adds sweetness through enzymatic breakdown.
notes: Contradicts common advice to add a little sugar to lean doughs for the yeast.

claim: Flip flatbread every 30 seconds during cooking so both sides get heat; stop flipping once it starts to inflate significantly, to avoid popping the bubble.
notes: Conduction makes the side against the pan hotter. Her cooking time per side is also given at 31:18.

claim: At 16% sugar (baker's percent), the yeast does not need an osmotolerant strain: the osmotic stress is real but not enough to cause a strongly delayed fermentation; the fermentation is just a bit longer.
notes: Contradicts common advice that doughs above roughly 10-15% sugar need osmotolerant yeast. Her own standard sugar is about 6%; she says Asian sweet breads often reach 25-30%, which she finds too sweet.

claim: Milk can replace under 25% of the water in a dough: this improves elasticity, chewiness and resilience; she caps the milk share at that level.
notes: Above 25% the paper reported negative effects. Contradicts her own tangzhong video, which replaces 100% of the tangzhong water with milk (see s10-034). Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper on milk replacement of water in bread (quoted in video at 10:04) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Total fat around 8-9% (baker's percent, including butter and milk fat) is at the upper end of the usual soft-bun range; the fat tenderises the bun and, with tangzhong, extends shelf life.
conditions: sweet bun with butter and milk
notes: Butter-only share is 10% of flour in the dough (25 g / 250 g); the total with milk fat is her figure.

claim: Cold butter-based cookie doughs must be chilled so the butter stays in its narrow pliable range; if the dough warms, it is hard to shape.
notes: Room temperature in her video was above that range (personal condition, not stated as fact).

claim: Sweet dough with 16% sugar ferments more slowly than usual; it should roughly double in size, which takes longer than a lean dough.
Tangzhong 35 bread with about 69% hydration went stale faster than tangzhong 20 bread; at about 73-74% hydration the tangzhong 35 bread stayed softer longer.
conditions: shokupan, same ingredients, same bake; her own single-batch test
notes: The hydration result rests on her own experiment with the changed hydration; the 74% and 73% figures are from the video and the description. Sample size is one bake per condition, so do not treat it as a general rule. Home side-by-side comparison shown in the video (single trial, not a controlled study).

claim: A high tangzhong share (over 30% of flour, around 60% hydration) can make bread stale faster, according to a 2004 thesis; the thesis also says the gluten network weakens as tangzhong denatures protein.
conditions: thesis experiment with total dough weight held constant
notes: Contradicts common advice that more tangzhong always means softer bread. Thesis used sensory panel (20 members) as well as texture analysis. Unresolved source(s): Kēyùwén, thesis on tangzhong (Chinese title: 湯種添加量與熟成條件對麵包品質之影響), 2004 [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Thesis conclusions for high-tangzhong dough: longer proof time, less tolerance of over-mixing or kneading, lower specific volume, and stronger wheat flavour.
notes: Unresolved source(s): Kēyùwén, thesis on tangzhong, 2004 [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Starch retrogradation during ageing is controlled by the water present during ageing, regardless of the water used in gelatinisation; so the final-dough water outside the tangzhong matters for staling.
notes: Quote is about starch in wheat gels; the video applies it to bread. Naito et al., 2005 in the description is not discussed in this passage.

claim: Hydration of the final dough should be optimal (about 73% for tangzhong 35): enough water so the tangzhong starch hydrates well, without weakening the final dough's gluten.
notes: Hydration of the recipe in the description: 275.4 g water on 375 g flour (73.4%). Recomputed from ingredients: 210 g tangzhong water plus 70 g milk x 0.87 = 270.9 g (72.2%); the difference is not explained in the transcript. Unresolved source(s): Japanese paper on tangzhong 35 hydration (not named in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: About 5% solid fat (baker's percent) gives the maximum bread volume; beyond that volume barely changes, and too much fat inhibits proof (brioche with over 50% butter is dense).
notes: Her description of the trend, not a fixed rule. Unresolved source(s): Review paper on fat in bread (cited in video; not named) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Solid fats raise bread volume more than oils: the fat crystals stick to gas-liquid interfaces and stabilise gas cells; oil droplets do not, and oil-based doughs show more holes in the gluten film and less volume.
conditions: butter or shortening vs liquid oil
notes: Brooker is cited in the references list at 0:00; the 6:35 and 7:12 passages paraphrase the mechanism. Smith and Johansson is listed in the video description as reference 1.

claim: Beta-prime fat crystals (smaller than beta crystals) are preferred for bread. Milk fat and butter are beta-prime; sunflower, soybean and coconut oils are generally beta.
notes: Polymorph assignments are as she states them; she does not give the source for each fat.

claim: Oil in bread gives a moister crumb but lower volume and a denser, harder loaf, so use oil with caution in pan breads where volume matters.
notes: Effect depends on the oil type; she cites a study in which coconut oil beat sunflower oil.

claim: In a pan-bread test, olive oil gave hardness and springiness similar to shortening, but lower loaf volume.
conditions: white pan bread with olive oil
notes: Olive oil is a flavour carrier for savoury breads. Shows why an oil-for-butter swap changes more than flavour. Unresolved source(s): Unnamed paper on olive oil in white pan bread (not named in video) [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Oil uptake during frying is inversely related to the moisture content of the finished fried product; wheat fried dough needs at least about 80% hydration for starch to gelatinise.
notes: The 80% figure is attributed to another unnamed paper; the speculation that tangzhong suits fried dough is hers.

claim: Tangzhong 20 with about 71% hydration suits fried dough: higher hydration gives a crispier, thinner crust; a lower hydration keeps better volume and handling.
notes: The 71% hydration comes from the Farinograph water absorption of yudane 20 in a paper she cites (not named).

claim: Above about 20% tangzhong flour, the gluten is too weak to hold an inflated fried dough; higher shares give flat beignets.
notes: Her own limit; tangzhong 30 and 40 were not used.

claim: Tangzhong can be made with 100% milk in place of water, which she says adds elasticity and water absorption to offset the weak gas retention of tangzhong dough.
conditions: beignet tangzhong, 50 g flour, 100 g hot milk
notes: Contradicts her melonpan video, where milk above 25% of water is not recommended (s10-017).

claim: Milk makes the dough less acidic and slows fermentation, but gives better temperature tolerance; to compensate she adds more instant yeast (half a teaspoon) and a little sugar.
notes: Yeast is given in teaspoons only; no gram weight stated.

claim: Most oil absorption in fried dough happens during the cooling phase after frying, not during frying itself.
notes: Her practice: drain on absorbent paper right after frying. Frying oil at 190 C, see s10-r05.

claim: Tangzhong and sourdough both weaken gluten: gelatinised starch interferes with the gluten-starch matrix, and sourdough acids and enzymes break gluten down over long fermentation; a long ferment can make the dough unable to hold itself together.

Adding a little instant yeast (1/8 tsp in her recipe) to a sourdough-tangzhong dough shortens fermentation, which limits proteolysis and acid buildup; sourdough improves gas retention but does not produce gas.
notes: Partly contradicts the usual advice that a pure sourdough needs no commercial yeast; she adds a little yeast for control, not for rise.

claim: A levain of about 6 hours at 29 C more than doubles in volume; a cooler room takes longer and a warmer room faster.
notes: Timing assumes 29 C; judge by volume and bubbles, not clock time.

claim: Raising tangzhong to 20% of flour and levain to 30% in the buns kept the balance of gelatinised and sourdough flour; the 20% tangzhong with 30% levain gave a softer, tastier sourdough.
notes: Her own side-by-side test; she did not measure volume or texture numbers, so the 'measured' label reflects a comparison, not a quantified result.

claim: Bread flour at about 13% protein is a good middle ground for a soft Asian loaf: lower protein (all-purpose) gives a denser loaf; too much protein gives an artisan-like, too-strong crumb.
notes: Protein percentage is for her flour; check your own flour's label.

claim: Tangzhong at 1:5 flour to water, heated to 60-65 C while stirring, gelatinises most of the water; it is ready when the mixture thickens fully.
notes: Her 1:5 ratio is wetter than the 1:2 she uses in other videos; both are stated by her.

claim: Ice water lowers the final dough temperature to slow fermentation in a warm kitchen, avoiding over-fermentation and flat loaves.
conditions: warm climate; the temperature is local to her kitchen
notes: Her kitchen temperature is personal; generalised here as a dough-temperature control.

claim: Butter goes in after the dough is kneaded, because fat interferes with gluten development; milk powder adds milk richness without changing the liquid balance.
notes: Consistent with rvWSBsQLZXM and hUKMgsUGKoU.

claim: Beat eggs and sugar for 5-6 minutes until pale and fluffy; the batter should leave a short trail when the whisk is lifted. Add the sugar right away so it does not sit on the eggs.
notes: Science-only: non-yeast brownie. Air from whipped eggs lightens the batter without making a sponge.

claim: Whisk cocoa powder into the still-warm melted chocolate and butter to bloom it and bring out chocolate flavour; cool the mixture before adding to the eggs so they do not cook.
notes: Science-only.

claim: Longer baking gives a cakier brownie and shorter baking a fudgier one; ovens vary, so check the bake yourself.
notes: Science-only; the recipe is not a bread, so no recipe record.

claim: Add butter after the gluten has formed: fat coats the flour and makes gluten form slowly, so adding it early can give a cake-like texture and a longer knead.
notes: Matches her cinnamon roll practice (s10-r08 steps).

claim: Fat competes with water for flour and coats gluten strands, so gluten forms more slowly and the crumb becomes finer and denser; at sufficient amounts, fat can film gas bubbles and increase volume.
notes: Mechanism explained without citation. Contradicts the common view that fat always lowers volume; she says it depends on the amount (see also 2:32).

claim: Solid fats such as shortening are said to improve bread volume more than liquid fats.
notes: Source not named in transcript; treat as her summary of the same literature as 7vLYCrhbgaU. Unresolved source(s): Not named in video ('have been shown') [literature claim without an identifiable paper]

claim: Butter contains some water, so count it in hydration when calculating a formula.
notes: Matches the calculator rule: hydration counts water in butter/milk.

claim: Oil on the bench and bowl prevents sticking and makes low-hydration dough easier to handle without adding flour; butter brushed on as a glaze melts into the crust, adding flavour and softness.
notes: Locator corrected from 6:31 to 7:09 after re-check.

claim: Yeasted muffin batter with poolish: after mixing, ferment 4 h at 26 C or 10-16 h in the fridge until it looks bubbly and aerated; the 26 C room is a condition of the 4 h time.
notes: Yeasted muffins are rare; she compares the flavour to bread.

claim: Mix the flour only until no lumps remain and stop immediately, to avoid overmixing.
Fill muffin cups to about 3/4 and let them rise 3-4 hours until the batter fills the cup, then bake at 180 C top and bottom for about 50 minutes.
conditions: muffin pans; times vary with oven

claim: Melted butter coats flour proteins and helps keep the crumb moist, and adds flavour; melt it fully and let it cool before adding.
Poolish of equal weights flour and water is mixed with chopsticks, covered, rested about 1 h at room temperature, then refrigerated overnight before use the next day.
conditions: room temperature not stated; the video says room-temperature poolish takes 2-3 h to mature
notes: Short video; only 2 claims extractable.

claim: A poolish left at room temperature takes about 2-3 hours to mature fully; she rests it 1 hour and then refrigerates it overnight.
notes: Room temperature is not given; timing depends on it.

claim: High-protein bread flour gives cinnamon-roll dough the strength to rise well.
Tangzhong keeps bread softer for longer and makes the dough easier to handle at higher hydration, because the gelatinised starch absorbs more water.
conditions: cinnamon-roll dough with tangzhong made beforehand
notes: Tangzhong method not shown in this video; she refers to earlier videos.

claim: Butter is added only after the dough has been kneaded for a few minutes, because fats interfere with gluten development; the butter is left out to soften first.
notes: Kneading before butter: 1 min low, then 3-4 min medium-high (2:46). Consistent with hUKMgsUGKoU 5:08.

claim: Windowpane test: stretch a small piece of dough thin enough to see light through it; the dough is ready when it lifts cleanly from the bowl and looks smooth and cohesive.
Bulk ferment about 1 h or until doubled; after shaping, proof 1 to 1.5 h until almost doubled; bake 30-35 min at 180 C top and bottom or until golden.
conditions: room temperature not stated; dough covered

source.locator: 6:33; proof and bake in later paragraphs (~"proof for an hour to an hour and half", 180 °C 30–35 min)
source.author: Novita Listyani

notes: Proof stated at 15:14; bake at 16:32. Time depends on room temperature.

claim: Roll the dough to about 0.5 cm thick, rolling from the centre outward and never to the edge; cut 8 pieces by halving three times.
conditions: rectangle of enriched dough with filling
notes: Rolling and cutting at 9:09 and 13:39.

claim: Her beginner sequence of bread-making steps: preferment, mixing, bulk fermentation, dividing, preshaping, bench rest, shaping, final proofing, baking, cooling.
notes: Video has no captions; step list from description only.

claim: Bakery α-amylases differ by origin: cereal amylase has low purity, medium heat resistance and many side activities; fungal amylase has medium purity and low heat stability; bacterial amylase has high purity and is extremely heat stable, which brings over-dose problems. Only cereal amylase registers in the falling-number test; fungal amylase does not.

source.locator: Amylase, section 'Comparative functionalities of amylases from various sources'
source.author: BAKERpedia

claim: BAKERpedia gives optimal conditions for α-amylase in dough as pH 5.5–6.0, 40–60 °C, at least 60 min of contact with the substrate and water activity of 0.9 or more; α-amylase only attacks damaged or gelatinised starch.
Added α-amylase is usually dosed at 0.002–0.006 % of flour weight (20–60 ppm).
conditions: commercial enzyme preparation; activity per gram varies by product

claim: In the IREKS table of processes during baking, β-amylase is inactivated at 60 °C, α-amylase at 75 °C, and enzymes in general above 80 °C; the yeast and acid-forming bacteria are inactivated at 50–60 °C.
conditions: temperature inside the dough piece during baking; flour (cereal) enzymes

source.locator: The baking process > Processes in the dough and the baked goods during the baking process, table 'Processes in the dough/baked goods during baking'
source.author: IREKS GmbH

notes: Trade compendium; the table is an image on the page, transcribed.

claim: In rye scalding, the optimum temperature is 72–74 °C for α-amylase and 60–65 °C for β-amylase, both within typical scald conditions.
conditions: malt and rye flour amylases in a rye scald

claim: Most bakery enzymes work at pH 4.0–7.5 and 35–60 °C, are dosed at 0.005–0.01 % of flour (50–100 ppm), and need contact time, water and substrate; reaction rates roughly double per 10 °C rise until the enzyme denatures.

IREKS summary of enzyme effects: amylases lower dough viscosity and feed the yeast (colour, volume); pentosanases/xylanases split insoluble carbohydrates, giving higher water binding, drier dough, more volume and better freshkeeping; proteases soften gluten and give a more tender, shorter crumb; lipases give more volume; hexose oxidases produce hydrogen peroxide that strengthens gluten and dries the dough.

claim: Bakery protease is dosed at 0.1–0.5 % of flour depending on product (e.g. 0.25 % powder or 75 haemoglobin units per 100 g flour), works best at pH 4.5–6.5, and in excess weakens the gluten so much that gas retention falls; it is mainly used in processes without long fermentation or sourdough.

Xylanase (EC 3.2.1.8) cuts the xylan backbone of arabinoxylans; partial breakdown of water-unextractable arabinoxylans into medium-to-high molecular weight water-extractable ones improves dough handling, gas retention, oven spring and crumb fineness, and releases water bound by the larger polymers (dough relaxation).

claim: Lipoxygenase is usually added as enzyme-active soy flour at no more than 0.5 %; it bleaches flour carotenoids (whiter crumb), co-oxidises proteins to strengthen the dough against over-mixing, and can create off-flavours if over-used.

Mills add ascorbic acid at 0.5–3.0 g per 100 kg flour (5–30 ppm). An enzyme of the flour converts it into dehydroascorbic acid, which oxidises the flour's glutathione and so stops glutathione from weakening the gluten; dough stability and gas retention rise.

source.locator: Improvers and mixes > Technological effect of additives > Ascorbic acid
source.author: IREKS GmbH

claim: In bread and buns ascorbic acid is used up to 150 ppm of flour; the US FDA limit is 200 ppm. It needs oxygen from mixing and the flour's ascorbate oxidase to act, competes with yeast and glucose oxidase for oxygen, and whole-wheat or multigrain doughs need more of it. Historical work reported about 20 % more volume at 20–30 mg/kg.
notes: BAKERpedia also states an EU/UK maximum of 200 ppm except wholemeal; that statement was not checked against EU law.

claim: Glucose oxidase oxidises glucose into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide; the peroxide strengthens gluten (disulphide and dityrosine cross-links, arabinoxylan gelation). It needs oxygen, so it acts mainly during mixing; the yeast soon uses up the dough's oxygen.

Most bakery lipases prefer pH about 8 and temperatures above 45 °C; they turn flour polar lipids into surface-active lysolipids. Over-dosing releases free fatty acids (rancid taste) and can break down the lysolipids again, with gas-cell coalescence and loss of oven spring.

Lowering whole-wheat dough to about pH 5.5, by sourdough or by adding lactic acid, broke down 70 % of the flour phytate, against 40 % without leavening or acidification: the wheat's own phytase, not the sourdough microbes, did most of the work.

Sourdough fermentation lowered phytate in whole-wheat bread by 62 %, yeast fermentation by 38 %; pre-incubating the bran with sourdough or yeast raised breakdown to about 90 %, whereas 40 % of the phytate remained in traditional French bread.
Endogenous cereal phytase works best at pH 4.3–5.5; an early sourdough study put the optimum for phytate degradation at pH 4.3–4.6.

source.locator: section on mineral bioaccessibility and Table (citing Fretzdorff 1992 and Leenhardt 2005)
source.author: Ribet et al.

claim: Long sourdough fermentation degrades much more phytate than short yeast fermentation, because acidification activates the flour's phytase and yeast has little phytase; whole-grain sourdoughs show the largest reductions; added fungal phytase (Aspergillus niger) can remove up to 100 %.

Roasting or cooking grain destroys its phytase, so fermenting cooked or roasted grain does not reduce phytate much; grains low in phytase (maize, rice, oats, millet) need longer fermentation or an addition of a high-phytase grain.

source.locator: section on fermentation and phytate (citing Egli et al. 2002, 2003)

EFSA excluded from its evidence base β-glucans that had been degraded, for example by enzymatic hydrolysis, to lower molecular weight or viscosity, because such degradation lowers their post-prandial glucose-lowering efficacy.

claim: BAKERpedia recommends 1.8–2.0 % salt (baker's %) in bread and 0.75–1.25 % in cookies and cakes, where it is only for flavour. In bread, salt tightens the gluten (the more salt, the stiffer the dough) and slows the yeast by osmosis.

Adding 1.5 % salt to 176 Italian soft-wheat flours (41 cultivars) lowered farinograph water absorption by a few percentage points in 95 % of samples, lengthened development time in 78 % and raised stability in 70 %, lowered softening in 72 %, and raised alveograph strength W by up to 86 %.
conditions: Brabender farinograph and Chopin alveograph, 0 vs 1.5 % NaCl

claim: 1.5 % salt (the average in Italian bread) was enough to improve medium-quality bread flours so they tolerate longer fermentation and mixing; strong flours performed well without salt and 3.0 % made them too tenacious. The authors conclude that more than 1.5 % salt is unnecessary for bread-making quality.
notes: Taste is not assessed; BAKERpedia's 1.8–2.0 % is a flavour-and-practice range.

claim: Salt's effect on fermentation rate is modelled in the fermentation model (modifier 'salt', from rheofermentometer gas data of the same study): about 4 % faster at 1.5 % salt and 12 % slower at 3 % than at 2 %.

Sugar feeds the yeast, sweetens, holds water (humectant, lower water activity), browns by Maillard reaction and caramelisation, and raises the temperature at which starch gelatinises and proteins denature; in short-time bread processes some fermentable sugar is needed for full proof and oven spring.

source.locator: Sugar, sections 'Function', 'Cake batters' and 'Bread and buns'
source.author: BAKERpedia

claim: Sweeteners raise the gelatinisation temperature of starch; wheat starch (onset 60.8 °C in water) is among the most affected. Fructose raises it least, isomalt and isomaltulose most, and the rise grows with concentration (tested at 0.5–4 M in a 2:1 solution:starch slurry).
notes: Quantitative shifts per sugar level are in the scalds/DSC part of the corpus (model-cereal.json).

claim: The slowing of yeast by high sugar levels (osmotic stress) is handled by the fermentation model's sugar modifier; osmotolerant instant yeast is the usual answer in sweet doughs.

Honey can replace sugar 1:1 by weight if the recipe's liquid is cut by 15–18 % of the honey weight; the oven should be about 14 °C cooler to limit browning. Honey's pH is 3.5–4.5, and fructose plus glucose make up 65–95 % of its carbohydrate.

Shortening is used at 3–5 % in bread to improve sliceability, moistness, volume and oven spring, up to 12 % in yeasted doughnuts; it shortens gluten strands and slows starch retrogradation. 100 g butter is replaced by 80 g shortening.
Butter is about 80 % fat; the remaining 20 % is water with milk solids. It interferes with gluten development, which makes baked goods more tender.

Compared with water, milk in a dough raises water absorption (softer dough), raises dough pH so fermentation is slower and more tolerant, browns faster (lactose), and gives more volume, a darker crust and longer shelf life. 100 g whole milk can be rebuilt from 8.5 g non-fat dry milk, 3.5 g butter and 88 g water.

Egg composition for bakers: liquid whole egg 75 % moisture (protein 53.2 %, fat 46.0 % of dry matter), liquid whites 88 % moisture, liquid yolks 49 % moisture (fat 62 % of dry matter), dried whole egg 5 % moisture. Eggs add colour, flavour, structure by protein coagulation, emulsification by yolk lecithin, and tenderness.

claim: Water content per 100 g (Ciqual 2020): pasteurised whole milk 89.1 g, semi-skimmed milk 89.4 g, raw whole egg 76.3 g, raw yolk 55.0 g, raw white 87.6 g, unsalted 82 %-fat butter 15.4 g, honey 17.6 g, skimmed milk powder 1.95 g, white sugar 0.17 g.

For hydration bookkeeping, count the water each ingredient brings: dough water = water + 0.89 × milk + 0.76 × whole egg + 0.55 × yolk + 0.88 × white + 0.15 × butter + 0.18 × honey + 0.21 × malt syrup. The dough will still feel softer than an all-water dough of the same hydration because fat and yolk tenderise and sugar competes for water.

Staling starts as soon as bread cools: water moves from the crumb to the crust and out, the crust loses crispness and the crumb firms. Amylose retrogrades already during cooling and sets the initial crumb firmness; amylopectin recrystallises slowly during storage and squeezes out water (synaeresis). Amylose retrogradation is irreversible; amylopectin retrogradation can be partly reversed by reheating ('crisping up'), which gives a short-lived impression of freshness.

Recrystallisation of bread starch is fastest around 0 °C. Freezing delays it; so would warm storage above 55 °C at about 80 % relative humidity, but that costs energy and risks spoilage. Freezing pre-baked and baked goods at −18 °C is the established practice.

Regular sourdough bread is not gluten-free: fermentation lowers gluten but not to 20 ppm or less, the US gluten-free limit. Beyond Celiac does not recommend sourdough for people with coeliac disease unless it is labelled gluten-free or made with gluten-free starter and ingredients, and notes that intestinal damage can occur without symptoms.

In the EU, 'gluten-free' may only be stated for food that contains no more than 20 mg/kg of gluten as sold, and 'very low gluten' for specially processed wheat, rye, barley or oat ingredients at no more than 100 mg/kg.

In a 60-day trial in people with coeliac disease eating 200 g of baked goods a day, ordinary wheat flour (80,127 ppm gluten) made 2 of 6 stop because of symptoms, with rising anti-transglutaminase antibodies and small-bowel deterioration; extensively hydrolysed flour (2,480 ppm residual gluten) caused no complaints but subtotal villous atrophy in both patients; only fully hydrolysed flour (8 ppm), made with selected sourdough lactobacilli plus fungal proteases, left antibodies and mucosa unchanged in 5 patients.

An acute challenge used a sourdough of 30 % wheat with oat, millet and buckwheat flours, fermented 24 h with selected lactobacilli and their extracts, about 2 g gluten per bread: 13 of 17 coeliac patients showed altered intestinal permeability after the yeast bread but not after this sourdough bread.

Sourdough fermentation does not make wheat, rye or barley bread safe for people with coeliac disease. Ordinary sourdough leaves gluten far above the 20 mg/kg gluten-free limit; the experimental breads that coeliac patients tolerated used selected lactobacilli plus fungal proteases (or mostly gluten-free flours) and reached 8 ppm, while partly hydrolysed flour at 2,480 ppm still damaged the intestine.

claim: Italian durum products (DPR 187/2001, art. 2), on dry matter: semola ash at most 0.90 %, protein at least 10.50 %, and at most 25 % of it may pass a 0.180 mm sieve; semolato 0.90–1.35 % ash, protein ≥ 11.50 %; semola integrale 1.40–1.80 %; farina di grano duro 1.36–1.70 %. Re-milled semola and semolato ('rimacinati') are allowed only for bread making and retail.
notes: Semola rimacinata has no separate ash limit: it is re-milled semola (≤ 0.90 %) or semolato.

claim: US 'flour' (21 CFR 137.105) is not typed by ash: its ash, on a moisture-free basis, may not exceed one twentieth of its protein (moisture-free) plus 0.35; moisture is at most 15 % and at least 98 % must pass a 212 µm sieve. All-purpose and bread flour are not separate standards of identity.
notes: Worked: 12 % protein (moisture-free) allows ash up to 12/20 + 0.35 = 0.95 %. Part 137 has no 'bread flour' or 'all-purpose flour' section.

claim: US whole wheat flour (21 CFR 137.200) keeps the proportions of all natural constituents of the wheat other than moisture; at least 90 % must pass a 2.36 mm sieve and at least 50 % an 850 µm sieve; moisture at most 15 %.

US semolina (21 CFR 137.320) is durum wheat ground so that it passes a No. 20 sieve with at most 3 % through a No. 100 sieve, with ash at most 0.92 % (moisture-free); durum flour (137.220) allows ash up to 1.5 %.

USDA SR Legacy (as is): all-purpose wheat flour 10.33 % protein, 0.47 % ash, 2.7 % fibre, 11.92 % water; bread flour 11.98 / 0.47 / 2.4 / 13.36; whole-grain wheat flour 13.21 / 1.58 / 10.7 / 10.74; cake flour 8.2 / 0.39 / 1.7; 'industrial 15 % protein' flour 15.33 / 0.53 / 2.4.

USDA SR Legacy (as is) for other milled grains: rye flour light 9.82 % protein / 0.78 % ash / 8.0 % fibre, medium 10.88 / 1.2 / 11.8, dark 15.91 / 2.5 / 23.8; spelt grain 14.57 / 1.78 / 10.7; Kamut khorasan grain 14.54 / 1.67 / 11.1; semolina 12.68 / 0.77 / 3.9; buckwheat whole-groat flour 12.62 / 2.54 / 10.0; oat flour (partly debranned) 14.66 / 1.97 / 6.5; barley flour 10.5 / 1.28 / 10.1; whole-grain corn flour 6.93 / 1.45 / 7.3; degermed corn flour 5.59 / 0.46 / 1.9; white rice flour 5.95 / 0.61 / 2.4; brown rice flour 7.23 / 1.54 / 4.6; dried unpeeled European chestnuts 6.39 / 2.4 / 11.7.

claim: US bread flour is a high-protein patent flour from hard red spring or winter wheat with 11.5–13.5 % protein (also given as 12–14 %, against about 11 % for all-purpose flour); all-purpose flour is milled from hard red wheat or an 80:20 hard:soft blend.
